--- description-meta: High-performance graph analysis library open-graph: title: Directed acyclic graphs | Edgecase description: High-performance graph analysis library twitter-card: title: Directed acyclic graphs | Edgecase description: High-performance graph analysis library gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} - >- ``{=html} title: Directed acyclic graphs guide-section: "Analysis" bread-crumbs: false --- A *directed acyclic graph*, or DAG, is a directed graph with no cycles: following its edges forward never leads back to the start. DAGs describe anything with an order of precedence. Tasks and their dependencies, courses and their prerequisites, the cells of a spreadsheet, packages in a build system, the commits of a version history, citations between papers, and causes and their effects all form DAGs, and the absence of cycles makes possible a family of methods that don't apply to graphs in general. This page covers those methods: ordering, scheduling and the critical path, ancestry and reachability, transitive closure and reduction, dominators, d-separation in causal diagrams, and the special case of trees. ## A project as a DAG The examples in the first part of this page use the plan for building a house. Each task has a duration in days, and some tasks can't start until others are finished. An edge from one task to another means that the first must be done before the second can begin, and each edge is weighted by the duration of the task it leaves, so that the length of a path is the time it takes to work through it. A final `done` node marks the end of the project: ::: {#dc000522 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec import polars as pl durations = { "survey": 3, "foundation": 5, "framing": 10, "plumbing": 4, "electrical": 5, "roof": 6, "insulation": 3, "drywall": 7, "painting": 4, "landscaping": 6, "inspection": 1, } depends_on = [ ("survey", "foundation"), ("foundation", "framing"), ("foundation", "landscaping"), ("framing", "plumbing"), ("framing", "electrical"), ("framing", "roof"), ("plumbing", "insulation"), ("electrical", "insulation"), ("insulation", "drywall"), ("roof", "drywall"), ("drywall", "painting"), ("painting", "inspection"), ("landscaping", "inspection"), ("inspection", "done"), ] house = ec.Graph.from_edges( [(before, after, durations[before]) for before, after in depends_on], directed=True, graph_name="House", ) house.is_dag() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: [`is_dag()`](../reference/Graph.is_dag.qmd) confirms that the plan has no circular dependencies. As on other pages, a small helper turns node IDs into task names: ::: {#a3d58b38 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def names(ids): return [house.get_label_from_id(i) for i in ids] ``` ::: ## Ordering A *topological order* lists the nodes so that every edge points forward: each task comes after all the tasks it depends on. Every DAG has at least one, and a graph with a cycle has none. [`topological_sort()`](../reference/Graph.topological_sort.qmd) returns one: ::: {#089d1177 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(house.topological_sort()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['survey', 'foundation', 'framing', 'landscaping', 'plumbing', 'electrical', 'roof', 'insulation', 'drywall', 'painting', 'inspection', 'done'] ``` ::: ::: Working through the tasks in this order never starts one before its prerequisites. A DAG usually has many topological orders, since tasks that don't depend on each other can be done in either order, and the one returned depends on how the graph was built. [`lexicographical_topological_sort()`](../reference/Graph.lexicographical_topological_sort.qmd) returns a canonical one, which at each step takes the available node with the smallest label (or the smallest value of `key=`), and so gives the same order however the graph was built. [`all_topological_sorts()`](../reference/Graph.all_topological_sorts.qmd) lists every order, of which this small plan has 64. [`topological_generations()`](../reference/Graph.topological_generations.qmd) groups the nodes into *generations* instead. The first holds the nodes with no predecessors, and each later generation holds the nodes whose predecessors all lie in earlier ones: ::: {#dda11432 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} [names(generation) for generation in house.topological_generations()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` [['survey'], ['foundation'], ['framing', 'landscaping'], ['plumbing', 'electrical', 'roof'], ['insulation'], ['drywall'], ['painting'], ['inspection'], ['done']] ``` ::: ::: The tasks in a generation don't depend on one another, so they can proceed at the same time: once the framing is up, the plumber, the electrician, and the roofers can all work at once. The generations are also a natural way to draw a DAG, in layers from left to right. [`layout_multipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_multipartite.qmd) places each generation in a column and stores the positions in a `pos` attribute: ::: {#66b2e970 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} generations = house.topological_generations() house.layout_multipartite(subset_key=dict(enumerate(generations))) house.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=10, width=700, height=300) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: If the graph has a cycle, every ordering method raises a `ValueError`. Suppose a mistaken dependency makes the plumbing wait for the painting, which itself comes after the plumbing: ::: {#93fa5cc7 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} broken = ec.Graph.from_edges(depends_on + [("painting", "plumbing")], directed=True) broken.is_dag(), [[broken.get_label_from_id(i) for i in cycle] for cycle in broken.simple_cycles()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` (False, [['painting', 'plumbing', 'insulation', 'drywall']]) ``` ::: ::: [`simple_cycles()`](../reference/Graph.simple_cycles.qmd) finds the offending loop, and [`minimum_feedback_edge_set()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_feedback_edge_set.qmd) finds the fewest (or, on a weighted graph, the lightest) edges whose removal would break every cycle. For a large graph with many cycles, [`condensation()`](../reference/Graph.condensation.qmd) collapses each strongly connected component into a single node, which leaves a DAG to which all of the methods on this page apply (see [Connectivity and flows](connectivity.qmd#directed-graphs)). ## The critical path How long will the house take? Tasks in parallel overlap, so the answer isn't the sum of the durations but the length of the longest chain of dependent tasks, the *critical path*. Any delay to a task on that path delays the whole project. [`dag_longest_path()`](../reference/Graph.dag_longest_path.qmd) finds it, using the edge weights as lengths, and [`dag_longest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.dag_longest_path_length.qmd) gives its length: ::: {#aaf35ab8 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(house.dag_longest_path()), house.dag_longest_path_length() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` (['survey', 'foundation', 'framing', 'electrical', 'insulation', 'drywall', 'painting', 'inspection', 'done'], 38.0) ``` ::: ::: The house takes 38 days, and the critical path runs through the electrical work rather than the plumbing or the roof. Longest paths are only well defined in a DAG, since in a graph with a cycle a path could go around it forever. A topological order makes it easy to work out more of the schedule by hand. Going forward through the order, each task can start as soon as all its predecessors have finished, which gives its earliest finish. Going backward, each task must finish in time for all its successors to start, which gives its latest finish. The difference is the task's *slack*, how long it can slip without delaying the project. [`get_predecessors()`](../reference/Graph.get_predecessors.qmd) and [`get_successors()`](../reference/Graph.get_successors.qmd) supply the neighbors: ::: {#766f5554 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} order = house.topological_sort() def duration(node): return durations.get(house.get_label_from_id(node), 0) finish = {} for node in order: start = max((finish[p] for p in house.get_predecessors(node)), default=0) finish[node] = start + duration(node) project_end = max(finish.values()) latest = {} for node in reversed(order): latest[node] = min( (latest[s] - duration(s) for s in house.get_successors(node)), default=project_end ) schedule = pl.DataFrame( { "task": names(order), "start": [finish[n] - duration(n) for n in order], "finish": [finish[n] for n in order], "slack": [latest[n] - finish[n] for n in order], } ) schedule ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

The plumbing can slip by a day and the roof by two without consequence, and the landscaping, which nothing else waits for until the final inspection, has more than three weeks to spare. Coloring the drawing by slack makes the critical path stand out: ::: {#a0d63c43 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} house.set_node_attrs( "schedule", {n: "critical" if latest[n] == finish[n] else "has slack" for n in order}, ) house.plot(layout="pos", color_by="schedule", label_by="label", node_size=10, width=700, height=300) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Ancestors and descendants In a DAG, a node's *ancestors* are the nodes from which it can be reached, and its *descendants* the nodes it can reach. [`ancestors()`](../reference/Graph.ancestors.qmd) and [`descendants()`](../reference/Graph.descendants.qmd) return them, and in a project plan they answer two everyday questions: what must be finished before a task can start, and what a delay to a task could hold up: ::: {#447204ce .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(house.ancestors("drywall")), names(house.descendants("plumbing")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` (['survey', 'foundation', 'framing', 'plumbing', 'electrical', 'roof', 'insulation'], ['insulation', 'drywall', 'painting', 'inspection', 'done']) ``` ::: ::: Before the drywall goes up, every earlier task except the landscaping must be done, and a delay in the plumbing could affect the insulation and everything after it. Both methods work on any directed graph, not only on DAGs, and [`descendants_at_distance()`](../reference/Graph.descendants_at_distance.qmd) limits the search to nodes a given number of steps away. ### Reachability queries Some applications ask whether one node can reach another many thousands of times on the same graph: whether one package depends on another, or whether one paper is in the citation history of another. [`has_path()`](../reference/Graph.has_path.qmd) runs a search for every question. [`reachability_index()`](../reference/Graph.reachability_index.qmd) does the work once, and returns a function that answers each question almost instantly by looking up two short lists: ::: {#49b89665 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} wiki = ec.wiki_vote() reaches = wiki.reachability_index() reaches(1, 2), reaches(2, 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` (False, True) ``` ::: ::: The function takes node IDs or labels, and here shows that a chain of votes leads from node 2 to node 1 but not back. On the Wikipedia election network, the index takes a few milliseconds to build and then answers each query in about a microsecond, thousands of times faster than a search. The index is a snapshot, so rebuild it after changing the graph. ### Lowest common ancestors The *lowest common ancestor* of two nodes is a node from which both can be reached and which is as close to them as possible. In a version history, where each commit points to the commits made on top of it, it is the *merge base*: the most recent commit that two branches share, which a version control system needs in order to merge them. Here is a history in which a feature branch (`f1`, `f2`) and a hotfix (`h1`) split off from the main line (`a1` to `a4`), and the feature was merged back in as `m`: ::: {#08fde779 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} history = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("a1", "a2"), ("a2", "a3"), ("a3", "a4"), ("a2", "f1"), ("f1", "f2"), ("a4", "m"), ("f2", "m"), ("a3", "h1"), ], directed=True, ) [ history.get_label_from_id(history.lowest_common_ancestor(x, y)) for x, y in [("a4", "f2"), ("m", "h1")] ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` ['a2', 'a3'] ``` ::: ::: The feature branch split off at `a2`, so that is the merge base of `a4` and `f2`. The merge `m` includes the main line up to `a4`, so its common ancestor with the hotfix is the later commit `a3`. [`lowest_common_ancestor()`](../reference/Graph.lowest_common_ancestor.qmd) returns one such node, [`all_lowest_common_ancestors()`](../reference/Graph.all_lowest_common_ancestors.qmd) returns them all (a DAG, unlike a tree, can have several), and [`all_pairs_lowest_common_ancestor()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_lowest_common_ancestor.qmd) answers many pairs at once. ## Closure and reduction The *transitive closure* of a directed graph adds an edge from every node to every node it can reach, and the *transitive reduction* of a DAG goes the other way, removing every edge that is implied by a longer path. A dependency list often contains redundant entries, such as a note that the roof depends on the foundation when it already depends on the framing, which depends on the foundation. [`transitive_reduction()`](../reference/Graph.transitive_reduction.qmd) removes them: ::: {#047cfcb6 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} redundant = ec.Graph.from_edges(depends_on + [("foundation", "roof")], directed=True) redundant.count_edges(), redundant.transitive_reduction().count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` (15, 14) ``` ::: ::: The reduction is the smallest graph with the same reachability, and the clearest one to draw. [`transitive_closure()`](../reference/Graph.transitive_closure.qmd) makes every indirect dependency explicit, which for the house turns 14 edges into 55: ::: {#8ae96d01 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} house.transitive_closure().count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` 55 ``` ::: ::: ### Antichains An *antichain* is a set of nodes none of which can reach another, such as a set of tasks none of which has to wait for another. The largest antichain is the most work that could ever be in progress at once, and its size is the *width* of the DAG. [`antichain_width()`](../reference/Graph.antichain_width.qmd) computes it, and [`antichains()`](../reference/Graph.antichains.qmd) lists every antichain: ::: {#e72f67eb .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} width = house.antichain_width() width, [names(chain) for chain in house.antichains() if len(chain) == width] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` (4, [['landscaping', 'plumbing', 'electrical', 'roof']]) ``` ::: ::: At most four crews could ever work at once on the house: the landscapers alongside the plumber, the electrician, and the roofers. By Dilworth's theorem, the width is also the fewest chains (sequences of dependent tasks) that together cover every node, and so the fewest workers who could complete the project if each worked through one chain. ## Dominators In a directed graph with a fixed starting node, a node `d` *dominates* a node `v` if every path from the start to `v` passes through `d`. The idea comes from compilers, which analyze programs as *control-flow graphs* of blocks of code, but it applies to any network with a source: a node's dominators are the points of failure that every route to it depends on. Here is the control flow of a simple loop, in which `test` decides whether to run the `body` again: ::: {#6ff6542c .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} program = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("entry", "init"), ("init", "test"), ("test", "body"), ("body", "update"), ("update", "test"), ("test", "exit"), ("body", "error"), ("error", "exit"), ], directed=True, ) label = program.get_label_from_id {label(node): label(dom) for node, dom in program.immediate_dominators("entry").items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` {'entry': 'entry', 'init': 'entry', 'test': 'init', 'body': 'test', 'update': 'body', 'exit': 'test', 'error': 'body'} ``` ::: ::: [`immediate_dominators()`](../reference/Graph.immediate_dominators.qmd) maps each node to its closest dominator, and these links form the *dominator tree*. Every run reaches `exit` through `test`, even though `exit` can also be reached through `error`, so `test` is its immediate dominator. The edge from `update` back to `test`, which leads to a node that dominates its own source, is a *back edge*, and it marks the loop. (This graph isn't a DAG; dominators are defined for any directed graph.) [`dominance_frontiers()`](../reference/Graph.dominance_frontiers.qmd) returns, for each node, the nodes where its dominance ends, which compilers use to decide where values from different branches must be merged. ## Causal diagrams and d-separation In a causal diagram, or *Bayesian network*, the edges of a DAG point from causes to their effects. The structure of the graph alone then says which variables are independent of which, given others. The rule is called *d-separation*: a set of nodes `Z` d-separates `X` from `Y` if it blocks every path between them, where a path is blocked at a node that is in `Z` and passes the path along (a chain or a fork), or at a *collider*, a node into which both of the path's edges point, that is *not* in `Z` and has no descendant in `Z`. The standard example has the season influencing both the rain and whether the sprinkler is on, either of which makes the grass wet, which makes it slippery: ::: {#73987598 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} lawn = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("season", "rain"), ("season", "sprinkler"), ("rain", "wet"), ("sprinkler", "wet"), ("wet", "slippery"), ], directed=True, ) [ lawn.is_d_separator("rain", "sprinkler", given) for given in [[], ["season"], ["season", "wet"], ["season", "slippery"]] ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` [False, True, False, False] ``` ::: ::: [`is_d_separator()`](../reference/Graph.is_d_separator.qmd) shows the rules at work. Rain and the sprinkler are linked through the season, so they are dependent until the season is known. Knowing the season makes them independent. But learning that the grass is wet, or merely that it is slippery, makes them dependent again, since wet grass on a dry day suggests the sprinkler was on: `wet` is a collider, and conditioning on it, or on its descendant `slippery`, opens the path. These rules are the basis of choosing which variables to adjust for in causal inference. [`find_minimal_d_separator()`](../reference/Graph.find_minimal_d_separator.qmd) finds a set that separates two nodes and has no smaller subset that also does, optionally restricted to the variables that were actually measured (`restricted=`): ::: {#485e8c55 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} [lawn.get_label_from_id(i) for i in lawn.find_minimal_d_separator("season", "slippery")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` ['rain', 'sprinkler'] ``` ::: ::: Knowing both rain and sprinkler blocks every path from the season to slippery grass. So does knowing whether the grass is wet, a different minimal set; minimal means only that no member can be dropped, not that the set is the smallest possible. [`is_minimal_d_separator()`](../reference/Graph.is_minimal_d_separator.qmd) checks a given set. ## Trees A *tree* is a connected graph without cycles, and so the simplest connected graph possible: it has exactly `n - 1` edges, and a single path between each pair of nodes. Its directed counterpart, an *arborescence*, has one root from which a unique directed path leads to every other node, like a family tree, an organization chart, or a file system. Trees appear throughout this guide, as search trees ([Traversals](traversals.qmd)), spanning trees ([Connectivity and flows](connectivity.qmd#spanning-trees)), and Steiner trees ([Paths and distances](paths.qmd#steiner-trees)), and many generators build them ([Generators](generators.qmd)). [`is_tree()`](../reference/Graph.is_tree.qmd) and [`is_forest()`](../reference/Graph.is_forest.qmd) test undirected graphs, and [`is_arborescence()`](../reference/Graph.is_arborescence.qmd) and [`is_branching()`](../reference/Graph.is_branching.qmd) (a directed forest) test directed ones. A tree can also be encoded compactly. A *Prüfer sequence* encodes a labelled tree on `n` nodes as a list of `n - 2` node numbers, and a *nested tuple* encodes the shape of a rooted tree, with each node's children inside its own parentheses: ::: {#f4d25293 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree = ec.Graph().add_balanced_tree(2, 2) tree.is_tree(), tree.to_prufer_sequence(), tree.to_nested_tuple(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` (True, [2, 2, 1, 3, 3], (((), ()), ((), ()))) ``` ::: ::: This is a binary tree of height 2, with a root, two children, and four grandchildren. [`from_prufer_sequence()`](../reference/Graph.from_prufer_sequence.qmd) and [`from_nested_tuple()`](../reference/Graph.from_nested_tuple.qmd) rebuild a tree from its code, which is useful for generating trees systematically or storing many of them. Nested tuples in canonical form (`canonical_form=True`) are equal exactly when two rooted trees have the same shape. Other methods for trees and branchings are these: | Method | Does | |---|---| | [`maximum_branching()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_branching.qmd), [`minimum_branching()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_branching.qmd) | find the heaviest or lightest directed forest in a weighted directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm) | | [`dag_to_branching()`](../reference/Graph.dag_to_branching.qmd) | unfold a DAG into a forest of its root-to-leaf paths, copying shared nodes | | [`Graph.join_trees()`](../reference/Graph.join_trees.qmd) | join several rooted trees under a new common root | | [`add_prefix_tree()`](../reference/Graph.add_prefix_tree.qmd) | build the prefix tree (*trie*) of a list of sequences, such as words | | [`lukes_partitioning()`](../reference/Graph.lukes_partitioning.qmd) | split a tree into connected clusters of bounded size, cutting as little edge weight as possible | | [`tree_decomposition()`](../reference/Graph.tree_decomposition.qmd), [`junction_tree()`](../reference/Graph.junction_tree.qmd) | organize a general graph as a tree of overlapping groups of nodes, the basis of many exact algorithms and of inference in probabilistic models | ## Summary | Question | Methods | |---|---| | Does the graph have cycles, and where? | `is_dag()`, `simple_cycles()`, `minimum_feedback_edge_set()` | | In what order can the nodes be processed? | `topological_sort()`, `lexicographical_topological_sort()`, `topological_generations()` | | How long is the longest chain of dependencies? | `dag_longest_path()`, `dag_longest_path_length()` | | What does a node depend on, and what depends on it? | `ancestors()`, `descendants()`, `reachability_index()` | | What do two nodes have in common? | `lowest_common_ancestor()`, `all_lowest_common_ancestors()` | | Which edges are redundant, and which are implied? | `transitive_reduction()`, `transitive_closure()` | | How much can happen in parallel? | `topological_generations()`, `antichain_width()` | | Which nodes must every route pass through? | `immediate_dominators()`, `dominance_frontiers()` | | Which variables are independent given others? | `is_d_separator()`, `find_minimal_d_separator()` |
